memory_update.text: LOPE is the reference university-partner platform for hybrid healthcare licensure capacity; supplied evidence links it directly to ABSN/OTA, simulation technology, virtual reality, and prerequisite strategies.
CVSA, formerly ATGE, is the obvious direct healthcare-education asset owner; ticker/name change in February 2026 should be tracked to avoid stale ATGE references.

APEI belongs in the underfollowed lane because Rasmussen University and Hondros College of Nursing create nursing/health-sciences exposure that may be obscured by APUS and military/online education labels.
HSTM is a second-order underfollowed supplier: healthcare workforce SaaS with nursing-school and nursing-student usage, plus historical simulation-education exposure through Laerdal/SimVentures.

Public pure-play simulation manikin, VR clinical lab, and clinical-placement software vendors were not clearly identified in this pass; many likely targets may be private, embedded inside larger companies, or not US-listed.
UTI should be tracked as an underfollowed healthcare licensure capacity name because Concorde's healthcare programs are hidden behind UTI's traditional automotive/skilled-trades label.
HSTM should be tracked as a second-order healthcare workforce infrastructure supplier, especially for learning, clinical development, credentialing, scheduling, onboarding, and compliance workflows.
RELX is a large-cap supplier reference rather than a pure underfollowed name; Elsevier's Shadow Health, HESI, SimChart, and VR nursing products map to simulation and licensure-readiness bottlenecks.

Public pure-play clinical simulation hardware vendors appear scarce; major names such as CAE Healthcare/Elevate, Laerdal, Gaumard, and several clinical-placement platforms require separate private-company mapping rather than US-listed stock inclusion.

For later layers, the key falsification tests are whether program growth is actually constrained by clinical placements/simulation/faculty versus demand, and whether vendors disclose material revenue exposure to nursing, OTA, counseling, or allied-health education.

HSTM should be prioritized in later layers as the clearest underfollowed public supplier to healthcare-licensure capacity because clinical rotations, credentialing, learning, onboarding, and student-health-system matching are directly tied to program throughput.

LOPE remains the best reference anchor for the ABSN/OTA/hybrid-program capacity node, supported by provided evidence on partner programs, simulation technology, VR, prerequisites, and licensure-linked fields.

ATGE is a direct healthcare-education capacity operator; later diligence should focus on clinical placement constraints, pass rates, employer partnerships, and federal student-aid/regulatory sensitivity.

Most pure-play nursing simulation vendors, including Laerdal, Gaumard, Elevate Healthcare/CAE Healthcare, Ascend Learning/ATI, UWorld, Relias, and many clinical-placement tools, appear private or embedded in large diversified parents; public-market mapping is therefore sparse and may require supplier/customer triangulation.
CAE should not be treated as current healthcare-simulation exposure after its February 2024 sale of CAE Healthcare to Madison Industries; keep it only as historical context or false-positive memory.

For this node, the chokepoint evidence to verify is not generic online enrollment; it is clinical rotation availability, simulation substitution allowances, program approvals, faculty/preceptor capacity, licensure outcomes, and employer-linked healthcare workforce pipelines.
LOPE is the reference operator for outsourced hybrid healthcare licensure capacity, especially ABSN/OTA, simulation, VR, and prerequisite-pipeline expansion.
ATGE is a direct healthcare licensure education reference name with Chamberlain, Walden, and medical/veterinary programs; monitor clinical partnerships and regulatory quality metrics.

HSTM is the strongest underfollowed second-order public supplier found in this pass because it maps to healthcare workforce learning, competency, credentialing, scheduling, nursing-school, and clinical-rotation workflows.
ZSPC belongs only in a speculative shadow lane: AR/VR healthcare simulation relevance is high, but micro-cap status, liquidity, and survivability must be falsified before further work.

Most pure-play nursing simulation vendors found in the search, including Laerdal, Gaumard, SimX, and several VR medical-simulation firms, appear private or not clearly US-listed; public-market mapping therefore shifts toward adjacent software, workforce infrastructure, and micro-cap immersive education names.

The strongest reference anchors are Grand Canyon Education and Covista, while the underfollowed lane contains American Public Education and HealthStream. The node appears investable through asset owners and service/platform operators that expand nursing, healthcare, social-work, counseling, and clinical-workforce training capacity. Simulation/VR hardware vendors remain mostly private or not clearly pure-play public, so the best public-market mapping in this pass is education operators plus healthcare workforce-learning software. The cleanest underfollowed supplier candidate is HealthStream, because it sits at the clinical-rotation, student-to-health-system, credentialing, and healthcare workforce software layer rather than the obvious university-operator layer.
